passage: The third time that week was in the hostel dining hall. Raghav, new in Vidya's house, passed her the dal and asked, "So where are you actually from? Like, really?" "Here. This city. I was born two streets from the school." "No, but originally?" Vidya smiled the smile she had practised. That morning a substitute teacher had told her, "Your English is so good," as if it were a surprise. On Monday the librarian had asked whether she'd "come on the scholarship". Taken one at a time, none of it was anything. Raghav wasn't being unkind; he looked honestly curious. But Vidya ate the rest of her dinner in silence, feeling like a visitor in the only place she had ever lived.

qa.q: Where was Vidya born?
qa.a: Two streets from the school, in this city.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she ate the rest of her dinner in silence?
qa.a: She felt out of place and alone, like a visitor in the only place she had ever lived, because Raghav's question was the third remark like it that week.

qa.q: What could Vidya choose to say the next time someone asks "originally?"
qa.a: She could calmly repeat that she is from here, or ask what makes them wonder, so she isn't swallowing it every time.

qa.q: How might Raghav see his question, compared with how it landed for Vidya?
qa.a: Raghav likely thought he was being friendly and curious, without knowing it was the third remark like that for her in one week.

grounding: A teenager hears repeated small remarks about where she is really from and how good her English is, and the build-up makes her feel like an outsider.

passage:
Dear Farhan,
City school, month two. The building has lifts! But I want to tell you the other thing.
On day one, a boy asked if we had electricity "back there". Last week Ma'am read my essay aloud and said, "Very good, especially for someone from a village school." Everyone clapped. Today in the lab a girl said, "You speak English so well, where did you learn?" I said, "In school, like you." She looked surprised.
None of them is cruel. I know that. But I keep counting them, like pebbles in my shoe. By evening my feet hurt from pebbles I can't show anyone.
Did anyone say things like this to you when you moved for college?
Tell your mother the essay was about her mango tree. Write soon.
Ganga

qa.q: What did Ma'am say after reading Ganga's essay aloud?
qa.a: "Very good, especially for someone from a village school."

qa.q: What does Ganga mean by "pebbles in my shoe"?
qa.a: Ganga feels each remark is tiny, but they keep piling up and hurting in a way that's hard to show anyone.

qa.q: What choice could Ganga make with these pebbles, rather than carrying them alone?
qa.a: Ganga could keep writing to Farhan, or tell a trusted teacher how the "especially for" comments feel, so the weight is shared.

qa.q: How might the girl in the lab have felt when Ganga said "In school, like you"?
qa.a: She may have been surprised, and perhaps briefly noticed that her question assumed something about Ganga.

grounding: A teenager new to a city school describes small, repeated remarks about a village background and English, adding up to feeling like an outsider.

passage: You want to know why I stopped answering in class, Sarita? It's not one big thing. It's small ones. My father sells vegetables near the station; everybody knows because he waves at the school bus. So when I topped the maths test, the teacher said, "Wah, a sabziwala's son, first!" Everyone laughed; he meant it as praise. Then the new coach asked if I'd need help with the fees before I'd even said anything. Then someone's mother at the parents' meeting said, "You speak so nicely!" like it was a trick. Each time I smile. Each time it's small. But by the end of the month I feel like I'm always being introduced as a surprise. Me, Vijay, a surprise. So today, after class, I finally told Ms Kurian, our class teacher. She listened, said it shouldn't be a joke, and she's talking to the maths teacher this week.

qa.q: What does Vijay's father do?
qa.a: He sells vegetables near the station.

qa.q: Why did Vijay stop putting his hand up in class?
qa.a: He was tired of being treated as a surprise; the small remarks piled up until speaking in class felt like inviting another one.

qa.q: What made telling Ms Kurian a good turning point?
qa.a: Vijay no longer carried it alone, and an adult who could act, by talking to the maths teacher, now knew about the pattern.

qa.q: How might the maths teacher see the "sabziwala's son" comment, and what could change after Ms Kurian talks to him?
qa.a: He likely thought it was praise; hearing how it landed might help him see that it marked Vijay out as an exception.

grounding: A teenager describes being repeatedly praised as surprisingly bright for his family background, small comments that add up to feeling singled out.

passage: I'm Sachin, and I sit behind Amandeep in our Year 10 form group in Leicester. I started keeping count after the careers fair. A visitor at the engineering stall shook his hand and asked, "And where are you really from?" Amandeep said, "Here. Born at the hospital down the road." The man laughed and waited, as if a better answer was coming. On Tuesday the new drama teacher told him his English was "lovely, so clear". He has never spoken anything else at school. On Thursday a supply teacher handed back his chemistry test, looked at the mark, then at him, and said, "Well! Didn't expect that." Each time, Amandeep smiled and gave a small nod. But on Friday, when our group was planning where to go after exams, he said, "Somewhere nobody asks where I'm from." Nobody laughed. I can't say what he felt exactly. I know he has stopped putting his hand up.

qa.q: Where was Amandeep first asked where he was really from?
qa.a: At the engineering stall at the careers fair.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's line about going "somewhere nobody asks where I'm from" suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests the small comments had piled up until he felt like an outsider in the town he was born in; Sachin noticed it didn't sound like a joke.

qa.q: After Friday, what choice does Sachin face, and what could make a difference?
qa.a: Sachin can keep counting silently or act on it, for example by checking in with Amandeep privately and, next time someone presses, backing up the first answer: "He said here."

qa.q: How might the visitor at the stall have seen the question, compared with how it landed?
qa.a: The visitor probably thought it was friendly curiosity, but by laughing and waiting for a 'better' answer, the man treated Amandeep's real home as not good enough.

grounding: A teenager born in the city is asked where he is really from, praised for his English and called surprisingly clever, and the small remarks add up to feeling like an outsider.

passage:
Monday, first week. Jaya had joined the private school in Class 11 on a scholarship. In the physics lab a boy leaned over her neat circuit and said, "Wow. Smart for a scholarship kid." Jaya laughed along. Her lab partner, Mehak, frowned but said nothing.
Two weeks later. The class teacher handed back the essays and smiled at Jaya. "Your English is really good, considering." Considering what, Jaya wanted to ask. At lunch a girl asked how she "managed" such marks "coming from there". Each thing was tiny. Jaya began eating her rotis in the library.
A month later. Mehak found her between the shelves. "You've stopped sitting with us." Jaya shrugged, then it came out. "Every day someone reminds me I'm the one who doesn't fit. Nobody means it. It's just every day." Mehak sat on the floor beside her and opened her tiffin. "Then tell me the next one when it happens. I'm listening."

qa.q: Where did Jaya start eating lunch?
qa.a: In the library, between the shelves.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she said, "Nobody means it. It's just every day"?
qa.a: She felt worn down and singled out; no single comment was big, but the steady repetition made her feel she didn't belong at the new school.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the third beat, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mehak came looking for Jaya and asked why she had stopped sitting with them, which let Jaya say the pattern out loud instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might the class teacher have meant "really good, considering", and how did it land for Jaya?
qa.a: The teacher probably meant it as warm praise, but for Jaya the word 'considering' was one more sign that people expected less of her.

grounding: A scholarship student hears one small remark after another about being clever or well-spoken for her background, and over weeks they add up to feeling like an outsider.

passage: Hansa, you came home quiet today. Did someone ask you again where you're "really" from? Sit with your Disha nani. When I was fifteen, my family moved from Imphal to Delhi. On the first day a teacher said, "Your Hindi is so good!" I smiled. The next day a girl asked, "But where are you really from?" I said Imphal. "No, originally?" I said Imphal again. In the market a shopkeeper spoke to me slowly, as if I couldn't understand. Each time it was small, a sting like an ant bite. But by the end of the month I felt I had a hundred bites. I stopped raising my hand. I thought, whatever I do, they'll see me as the girl from somewhere else. It was my friend Rukmini who just asked me what music I liked. That was the first day in Delhi I felt like a person, not a place.

qa.q: What did the teacher say on Disha's first day?
qa.a: The teacher said, "Your Hindi is so good!"

qa.q: How did Disha feel after a month of these remarks?
qa.a: Disha felt singled out and weary, as if covered in a hundred small bites, and began to feel like a permanent outsider.

qa.q: Why was Rukmini's question about music a turning point in the story?
qa.a: It treated Disha as a person with her own tastes rather than someone from somewhere else, which eased the outsider feeling.

qa.q: How might the girl who kept asking "where are you really from?" have seen her question?
qa.a: She probably thought it was harmless curiosity, not realising that repeating it made Disha feel she didn't belong.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a teenager in a new city, repeated small remarks about origin and language that each stung and added up to feeling like an outsider.

passage: Results day at the private school in Nagpur was chaos: rain hammering the tin shed, parents crowding the notice board, the printer jammed. Suraj, fifteen, the scholarship student from the municipal colony, pushed through to find his name: first in science. A teacher patted his shoulder. "Wow, Suraj! So smart, for someone from your background." A parent nearby said, "Scholarship boy? Really?" Suraj smiled politely. It was the third time that week. On Monday, someone had asked if his father "worked here" when he came to drop him. On Wednesday, a classmate had been surprised he spoke good English. Each comment was small. But standing under the dripping shed, holding his result, Suraj felt oddly alone. His friend Ujjwal nudged him. "First! Treat!" Suraj laughed, but the word "background" kept ringing in his ears.

qa.q: What rank did Suraj get in science?
qa.a: Suraj was first in science.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling as he stood holding his result?
qa.a: Suraj felt oddly alone and singled out, the small comments adding up to feeling like an outsider despite his success.

qa.q: What could the teacher have said instead?
qa.a: The teacher could simply have said, "Well done, Suraj, you worked hard," praising the result without tying it to his background.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see results day compared with Suraj?
qa.a: Ujjwal seems simply happy and proud of his friend, possibly unaware of how the comments were stinging Suraj.

grounding: A scholarship student is repeatedly praised as surprisingly smart for his background, and the small remarks add up to feeling like an outsider, on a chaotic results day.

passage: Dilnaz, sixteen, had moved from Srinagar to Pune two years ago. On Monday, in the canteen queue, a senior said, "Your English is really good. Did you learn it here?" On Tuesday, a new teacher asked, "Where are you actually from?" and when she said Pune, asked again. On Thursday, in the bus, a girl told her, "You don't even look Kashmiri," as if it were praise. None of them were rude. Some of them smiled. But by Friday, Dilnaz sat in the back of the classroom with her hood up. Her friend Vasudha slid in beside her. "What's up?" Dilnaz shrugged. "Nothing. Just... every day someone reminds me I'm from somewhere else." Vasudha was quiet, then said, "I didn't notice. I'm sorry. Tell me when it happens?" Dilnaz nodded. It helped a little to be heard.

qa.q: What did the girl on the bus tell Dilnaz?
qa.a: The girl told her, "You don't even look Kashmiri," as if it were praise.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling by Friday?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt tired and singled out, as if every small remark reminded her that she was an outsider.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that helped?
qa.a: Vasudha listened, apologised for not noticing, and asked Dilnaz to tell her when it happens, showing support without fuss.

qa.q: How might the teacher who asked twice see the question?
qa.a: The teacher probably thought it was friendly curiosity, not realising how often Dilnaz hears it.

grounding: A teenager hears repeated small remarks about her English, looks and origin, and though each is minor, they add up to feeling like an outsider.

passage:
When I moved from my small town to a Bengaluru school in Class 9, I heard the same sentence again and again. I'm Rehana. "Your English is so good for a girl from a small town!"
The first time, from a teacher, I said thank you. The second time, from a parent at a meeting, I smiled. By the tenth, I stopped smiling.
My friend Lakshmi once said, "They're complimenting you." And maybe they were. But every compliment came with a surprise attached. As if I shouldn't be able to.
It wasn't one big thing. It was a hundred small things that told me I didn't quite belong.
Now I read aloud in class anyway. Loudly.

qa.q: What sentence did Rehana hear again and again?
qa.a: "Your English is so good for a girl from a small town!"

qa.q: What did Rehana feel by the tenth time?
qa.a: Rehana felt tired and hurt, sensing each compliment carried surprise that Rehana could speak well.

qa.q: What could help someone like Rehana in a new school?
qa.a: Friends and teachers who notice the pattern and stop adding surprise to compliments, and a safe person like Lakshmi to talk it through with.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi seem to see the comments?
qa.a: Lakshmi sees them as compliments, perhaps not noticing the repeated surprise that makes Rehana feel like an outsider.

grounding: Shows a teenager repeatedly told her English is good for a small-town girl, where small remarks add up to feeling she doesn't belong.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11
Suraj, a scholarship student, came in today. He topped the physics test. He said that since then, classmates keep saying, "Wow, you're surprisingly smart," and one boy, Uday, said, "You're so sharp for someone from your area."
Suraj said, "They think it's praise. But why 'surprisingly'?"
He said it's never one big insult. It's the small sentences, every few days. He's started sitting at the back so nobody notices his marks.
I told him his feelings made sense. With his permission, I'll speak to the class teacher about a session on how compliments can carry assumptions. I'll also check in with him next week.

qa.q: Which test did Suraj top?
qa.a: He topped the physics test.

qa.q: Why has Suraj started sitting at the back?
qa.a: He feels singled out and uncomfortable, tired of hearing that his success is surprising.

qa.q: How could the counsellor's plan help?
qa.a: A class session could help students see how such compliments carry assumptions, and the check-in shows Suraj he is supported.

qa.q: How might Uday see his own comment?
qa.a: Uday probably thought it was a compliment, not realising it suggested Suraj's area makes him less likely to be smart.

grounding: Shows a teenager repeatedly praised as surprisingly smart for his background, small remarks that add up to feeling like an outsider.

Saturday
At Anand's birthday today his aunt asked me where I'm from. I said Pune. She laughed. "No, no, where are you really from?" So I said my parents are from Imphal, and she said, "Oh! Your Hindi is so good!" I've lived here since I was two. Then someone's cousin asked if I eat dogs, as a joke. Anand told him to shut up, which was nice. None of it was mean, exactly. Everyone smiled. But it's the fourth "really from" this month, and every time I feel like I'm standing outside a glass window, looking in at a party I'm supposed to be part of. I didn't eat much cake. I just want to be from here without explaining.
— Himani

passage: Every morning Mahima crossed the river on the ferry from the hamlet to the kasba high school, her notebook wrapped in plastic. The teachers liked her. That was part of the trouble. "Your English is so good, for someone from across the river," the English teacher said in front of the class. The next week, Lalit asked, grinning, "Do you people even have electricity there?" Another girl asked if her father could read. Each time Mahima smiled and answered. Nobody seemed to notice how many times it was happening. On the ferry home, watching the brown water, she counted them: seven, just this month. None of them was cruel. Together, they made the school feel like a place she was only visiting.
